title: Say No to Corporate Giveaways and Yes to Affordable Housing in the Railyards
description: Sacramento is proposing a $222 million taxpayer subsidy for wealthy developers in the Railyards, a plan that only has 6% affordable housing. 6% affordable housing is shamelessly inadequate. Sacramento deserves better!   Last year, a clear majority of Railyards residents protested the $92 million EIFD (Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District) subsidy, which forced the termination of the subsidy proposal under California law. Now, a year later, Sacramento is bringing the same bad deal, but with all residents drawn out of the plan boundaries to try to take away ability to reject the proposal. Instead of improving the plan, Sacramento is trying to undemocratically silence residents.    Sacramento must stop putting wealthy developers before everyday residents struggling with housing affordability. The City is facing an affordable housing crisis. The Railyards redevelopment will double the size of downtown Sacramento. If our city leaders really take housing affordability and homelessness seriously, this is their biggest opportunity to set us on a new path.

name: Legal Aid with Legal Fees
title: Application for the payment of costs - Legal Aid | Joshua Pietras
description:
How to get costs against Legal Aid Services….

Ahhh legal aid. The government slush fund for legal fees that is perpetually on life support. A system that was intended to help low-income individuals with access to justice but is now more broken than ever. 
  
If, by some miracle, you manage to obtain legal aid, well done, "you go Glen Coco". It can now be deployed as both a sword and a shield.
 
The legal aid ‘sword’ allows a party to advance their case in a way that would simply not be possible if they had to fund it themselves: 
  
·       Plead every cause of action under the sun? Sure. 
·       File that interlocutory application? Why not. 
·       Need funding for an expert witness in dog psychiatry? Most definitely. 
 
The legal aid 'shield' is even more powerful than the sword. Ordinarily, the unsuccessful party in litigation is required to pay the successful party’s legal costs. But not so when you’re on legal aid.  
  
Unless the legally aided party has acted egregiously, there is very little chance of an adverse costs award being made against them. And even if you get a costs order, there is little chance they’ll be able to pay it. 
  
However, there is a potential avenue for getting your costs paid. If the losing party would have been on the hook for costs ‘but for’ their legal aid status, you can ask the Court to certify what the costs order would otherwise have been.  
 
At first blush, this might seem like a pointless exercise. But there is a method to the madness. 
 
Under section 46 of the Legal Services Act 2011, the successful party who has been prejudiced by the immunity against costs can apply to Legal Aid Services and ask that it pay the costs that the Court has already certified would have been payable. 
  
When faced with one of these applications, Legal Aid must have regard to the following matters:
  
(a) the conduct of the parties to the proceedings.
(b) the court’s findings on the issue of ‘exceptional circumstances’.
(c) the hardship that would be caused if the costs were not paid by Legal Aid. 
  
The trick to all of this is to put Legal Aid on notice at a very early stage. If you think that the legally aided party is behaving badly, then write to Legal Aid and set out your concerns, making it clear that costs will be an issue if it continues to fund the proceedings. 
  
Then, when it turns out you were right, you can pull out that letter and lodge it alongside your application for costs, and say, “told you so”. 

I’ve only needed to do this once and was fortunately successful. 
  
Of course, this is not to say that all legally-aided parties are vexatious. In fact, the overwhelming majority of them conduct themselves appropriately. So it is best to keep this option reserved for exceptional case where the legal aid receipient has acted terribly. 
  
Attaching the relevant form here as it is quite hard to find online.
